doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Criticism of jazz education and the pre-Parker tradition
summary: Jazz methods ignore earlier players like Armstrong and Goodman; Weatherbird Rag as innovation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah. When you say you can’t teach jazz, how do you respond or react to all the jazz methods and the university programs and all that kind of thing that are out there now?

Well I think they’re all very good. I think you can teach the basics, the understanding. My biggest problem with most of them is that somebody writes a book and says here are all Charlie Parker’s solos. Once you learn these then you’ll be a jazz player. I mean it doesn’t really work that way. And they don’t really put enough emphasis on listening to people, listening to players that came before. My biggest problem with most jazz education programs is they act like nothing happened before Charlie Parker or Dizzy Gillespie. And there was a lot of great music being made. There was Louis Armstrong, there was Benny Goodman, I mean Jack Teagarden, guys who created great things from nothing. Charlie Parker and Dizzy will tell you the first thing that they did is they listened to — Dizzy listened to Roy Eldridge, Charlie Parker listened to Lester Young and Jimmy Dorsey. But these people, they don’t really want to know that there was anything going
on before that. I mean if you want to hear something innovative put on Louis’ duet record with Earl Hines doing “Weatherbird Rag.” It’s the most amazing thing I’ve ever heard.
And it’s like you said, it came from nothing.
That’s right. They didn’t have anybody to listen to. They came up with it all by themselves.
